claims.text: The baseline can be a homogenized, single-phase equiatomic NiCoCr-like alloy with minimal local chemical ordering.
A minor microalloying addition can intentionally increase compositional heterogeneity in a NiCoCr-like concentrated alloy.
An atomic-size-mismatched addition such as Sn can increase local lattice distortion in the proposed baseline alloy.
The minor addition can increase heterogeneity and distortion without changing the alloy's single-phase stability.
Greater compositional heterogeneity increases local chemical short-range ordering or hard atomic motifs.
Greater local compositional heterogeneity and lattice distortion increase spatial fluctuations in planar or shear-fault energy.
Local lattice distortions hinder or pin dislocation motion.
Spatial fluctuations in shear-fault energy are a primary source of strength in complex concentrated alloys.
Local hard atomic motifs provide the physical basis for the strength associated with fault-energy fluctuations.
Chemical short-range order can substantially change dislocation-slip behavior in CrCoNi.
The proposed microalloyed alloy will have greater yield strength than the unmodified baseline.
The proposed microalloying will produce more wavy or jerky dislocation motion than in the baseline.
The microalloyed variant will retain similar ductility to the baseline.
The microalloyed variant will remain single-phase under the proposed processing and test conditions.
The proposed mechanism should apply when the compared alloys remain single-phase and receive controlled, identical processing.
Phase separation, precipitation, or other microstructural instability could make the proposed mechanism inapplicable.
Failure to observe increased yield strength, altered dislocation behavior, or correlation between distortion and mechanical enhancement would falsify the hypothesis.
